assertions.text: Over the half-century to 1982, loser portfolios of 35 NYSE stocks outperformed the market by an average 19.6 per cent in the thirty-six months after portfolio formation, while winner portfolios earned about 5.0 per cent less than the market. The difference in cumulative average residual return between the extreme portfolios was 24.6 per cent, with a t-statistic of 2.20.
The effect is asymmetric: it is much larger for losers than for winners.

The more extreme the formation-period returns, the larger the subsequent reversal. Across seven specifications in Table I, the difference in cumulative average residual grows with the formation-period extremity: with a five-year formation period and 50-stock portfolios over 10 independent replications it reaches 0.319 at 60 months (t = 3.28); with sixteen three-year replications and 35-stock portfolios it reaches 0.246 at 36 months (t = 2.20).
Boundary condition: at a one-year formation period no reversal is observed at all, and the 49 one-year replications show -0.076 at twelve months (t = -2.32).

The effect occurs mostly in the second and third year of the test period. Twelve months into the three-year test the difference between the extreme portfolios is 5.4 per cent with a t-statistic of 0.77 -- not significant. A test run over one year would have found nothing.

The conclusion states the result as: prior losers outperform prior winners, with the losing stocks earning about 25 per cent more thirty-six months after formation, even though the winners are significantly more risky.

summary: The paper's central finding: portfolios of stocks with the most extreme prior losses outperform portfolios of prior winners over the following three years, by an amount that grows with how extreme the prior move was. One study, one dataset, one independence group -- the figures below are a single test, not a replicated result, and the paper predates the replications and challenges that followed.
title: The winner-loser reversal (De Bondt and Thaler, 1985)

assertions.text: Overreaction is defined against a norm rather than by intuition. Probability revision problems have a well-established norm because Bayes' rule prescribes the correct reaction to new information, and the term overreaction carries an implicit comparison to a degree of reaction considered appropriate.

In revising their beliefs, individuals tend to overweight recent information and underweight prior or base-rate data. Kahneman and Tversky describe the operative rule of thumb as one where the predicted value is selected so that the standing of the case in the distribution of outcomes matches its standing in the distribution of impressions -- an instance of the representativeness heuristic, which violates the principle that the extremeness of predictions must be moderated by considerations of predictability.

The finding survives the two obvious objections: Grether replicated it under incentive-compatible conditions, and there is considerable evidence that the actual expectations of professional security analysts and economic forecasters display the same overreaction bias.

Excessive market reaction to short-run news was described decades before it was measured. Keynes held that day-to-day fluctuations in the profits of existing investments, obviously ephemeral and nonsignificant, tend to have an altogether excessive and even absurd influence on the market; Williams held that prices have been based too much on current earning power and too little on long-term dividend paying power; Arrow concluded that Kahneman and Tversky's work typifies very precisely the excessive reaction to current information that seems to characterize all securities and futures markets.
These older statements are testimony, not measurement. Their value is showing the hypothesis predates the test, and they should not be counted as evidence for it.

summary: The psychological claim the market test was built to check, and the older observations of the same pattern in markets. Unlike the rest of this corpus the premise rests on several independent sources -- but they are reported here as De Bondt and Thaler characterize them; the primary studies are not in this corpus.
title: Overreaction: the behavioral premise behind the winner-loser reversal

assertions.text: Prediction 1: extreme movements in stock prices will be followed by subsequent price movements in the opposite direction. Prediction 2: the more extreme the initial price movement, the greater will be the subsequent adjustment. Both imply a violation of weak-form market efficiency, because if prices systematically overshoot the reversal is predictable from past return data alone, with no accounting data such as earnings.

The authors set their own standard: to test whether the overreaction hypothesis is predictive -- whether it does more than explain, ex post, the P/E effect or Shiller's results -- and claim these are the first tests to use a behavioral principle to predict a new market anomaly.

Two extensions are offered as conjecture and not tested here: that investor overreaction may explain Shiller's finding that long-term rates high relative to short rates tend to move down later, and Ohlson and Penman's suggestion that increased return volatility after stock splits may be linked to overreaction.

Open question the paper does not answer: how the anomaly survives arbitrage, and more generally what the equilibrium conditions are for markets where some agents do not revise expectations by Bayes' rule. Russell and Thaler conclude that the existence of some rational agents is not sufficient to guarantee a rational expectations equilibrium in an economy containing quasi-rational agents. The authors state they do not have the space to address this and concentrate on the empirical test instead.

summary: The two testable predictions, the standard the authors set for themselves, and the theoretical question they explicitly leave open.
title: What the overreaction hypothesis predicts, and what it does not settle

assertions.text: The design inverts the usual event study. Conventional semistrong tests form portfolios at t = 0 on an event affecting all stocks in the portfolio, such as an earnings announcement, then ask whether the later residual return is zero. This study asks instead whether systematic residual return behavior after formation is associated with systematic residual returns in the preformation months.

Winner and loser portfolios are formed conditional upon past excess returns rather than on a firm-generated informational variable such as earnings, focusing on stocks with extreme capital gains or extreme losses over periods up to five years.

The competing hypotheses as testable signs: market efficiency implies the expected residual return of both the winner and the loser portfolio, conditional on the information set at t-1, is zero. Overreaction implies the winner portfolio's expected residual is negative and the loser portfolio's is positive.

Data: monthly returns for NYSE common stocks from the CRSP file at the University of Chicago, January 1926 to December 1982. An equally weighted arithmetic average rate of return on all CRSP-listed securities serves as the market index.

Step 1: for every stock with at least 85 months of return data without missing values in between, starting January 1930, estimate the next 72 monthly residual returns; if data beyond month 85 are missing, calculate up to that point. Repeat 16 times, starting January 1930, January 1933, and so on to January 1975.

Step 2: from December 1932, compute each stock's cumulative excess return over the prior 36 months, repeating for all nonoverlapping three-year periods to December 1977. Rank the cumulative excess returns low to high; the top 35 stocks (or top 50, or top decile) form the winner portfolio and the bottom 35 (or 50, or decile) the loser portfolio.

Step 3: for both portfolios in each of the 16 periods, compute cumulative average residual returns over the next 36 months. If a security's return is missing in any month after formation, the stock is permanently dropped from that point and the CAR averages the available residual returns -- so every reported portfolio is implicitly rebalanced.

Steps 4 and 5, the statistics: average the CARs across the 16 replications for each month t = 1 to 36. Overreaction predicts the winner average is negative, the loser average positive, and their difference positive. Significance for the difference uses a pooled estimate of the population variance; with two samples of equal size N the variance of the difference of sample means equals 2S²/N. A separate one-sample t-statistic tests whether an individual month's average residual return differs from zero.
Limit on reading the statistics: t-statistics can be computed for each of the 36 postformation months, but they do not represent independent evidence.

summary: The procedure, in enough detail to reproduce or to attack. The design is the paper's contribution as much as the result: it conditions on past returns rather than on a corporate event, which is what makes a positive finding a weak-form violation.
title: Testing overreaction on past returns: the De Bondt-Thaler research design

assertions.text: Three residual types were computed -- market-adjusted excess returns, market model residuals, and excess returns relative to the Sharpe-Lintner CAPM -- because a study of specific portfolios over periods as long as a decade cannot simply assume that model misspecification leaves the conclusions unchanged. All three are single-index models following from the CAPM, so the authors concede misspecification may still confound the results.

Only market-adjusted excess returns are reported. The residual is the stock's return minus the market return, with no risk adjustment except for movements of the market as a whole, identical for all stocks. Because the same constant market return is subtracted from every stock's return in a period, the results are interpretable in raw dollar returns.

The general defense of any equilibrium model: as long as the variation in the market's expected return is small relative to movements in the residual, the exact specification makes little difference to tests of market efficiency, because even the correct model would explain only a small part of the variation.

The authors argue the market-adjusted choice biases the research design against the overreaction hypothesis, and report that winner and loser portfolios formed this way do not systematically differ in market value of equity, dividend yield or financial leverage. Both claims rest on De Bondt's separate unpublished dissertation, not on this paper, and cannot be checked from it.

The same applies to the robustness claim: the authors state that results using market model and Sharpe-Lintner residuals are similar and insensitive to using December as the formation month, while stating in the same sentence that those results are not reported here. Treat this as asserted, not demonstrated.

summary: The residual-return choice behind every percentage the study reports, its stated advantage, and the parts of the defense that rest on an unpublished dissertation rather than on this paper.
title: How returns were measured, and why the authors say it works against them

assertions.text: Survivorship: because the study concentrates on companies with extraordinary returns, their attrition rate might deviate from normal. The authors judge the concern unjustified on the mechanism: when a security is delisted, suspended or halted, CRSP determines whether it can be traded at the last listed price; failing that it seeks a subsequent quote; and if no quote exists because shareholders receive nothing, the return is entered as minus one.

Selection: requiring 85 subsequent returns biases the sample towards large, established firms. The authors argue this strengthens rather than weakens the result, since it counters the critique that overreaction is mostly a small-firm phenomenon. Between 347 and 1,089 NYSE stocks participate in the various replications.

Data frequency: monthly rather than daily data were chosen to avoid measurement problems that arise with daily data for both risk and return variables, including the bid-ask effect and the consequences of infrequent trading.

Window length: the 36-month test period is a compromise between an adequate number of independent replications and a period long enough to matter for asset pricing. It also matches Benjamin Graham's contention that the interval required for a substantial underevaluation to correct itself averages approximately one and a half to two and a half years. Selected experiments use one-, two- and five-year periods, and the number of independent replications varies inversely with formation length.

Formation month: choosing December, and therefore January as the starting month, is described as essentially arbitrary. Some tests use May as the formation month to check whether the choice affects the results.

summary: The threats to the result, each stated by the authors with their reasoning attached. These are the questions a critic asks, and the paper already contains its answers -- which is not the same as the answers being right.
title: Known weaknesses of the De Bondt-Thaler design

assertions.text: For all the experiments in Table I, the average CAPM betas of the securities in the winner portfolios are significantly larger than those of the loser portfolios. For the three-year experiment the betas are 1.369 and 1.026 respectively, with a t-statistic on the difference of 3.09. The betas are estimated from the market model over the 60 months prior to portfolio formation.

If the CAPM is correct, the loser portfolios therefore not only outperform the winner portfolios but are also significantly less risky, so the reported results are likely to underestimate both the true magnitude and the statistical significance of the overreaction effect.
The bias is worst for the winner portfolio: the residual calculations assume its CAPM beta equals 1.00 rather than 1.369.
The authors suggest this systematic bias may be responsible for the observed asymmetry between the portfolios. That is offered as a possibility, not a demonstration.

summary: The result that makes the reversal hard to dismiss as compensation for risk, and the measurement bias it implies.
title: The loser portfolios are less risky, not more

assertions.text: Most of the loser portfolio's excess returns are realized in January. In months t = 1, t = 13 and t = 25 the loser portfolio earns excess returns of 8.1 per cent (t = 3.21), 5.6 per cent (t = 3.07) and 4.0 per cent (t = 2.76).
In a five-year experiment the January effect on the loser portfolio is observed as late as five Januaries after portfolio formation.

The loser portfolio also tends to decline in value relative to the market between October and December, which agrees with the naive version of the tax-loss selling hypothesis, while the winner portfolio gains value at year end and loses some in January.

The authors state twice -- in the results and again in the conclusions -- that several aspects of the results remain without adequate explanation, most importantly the large positive excess returns earned by the loser portfolio every January, and that the five-year persistence came as a surprise to them. This admission is part of the finding, not an aside.

The overreaction effect is nonetheless qualitatively different from the January effect: the three-year formation experiment's difference in average cumulative residual exceeds the two- and one-year experiments' throughout the test period, although all three are affected by the same underlying seasonal pattern.

summary: The corpus's most striking result and the one the authors say they cannot account for. Its persistence over five successive Januaries is what breaks the standard tax-loss selling explanation.
title: The January effect in loser portfolios, unexplained

assertions.text: Winner and loser portfolios were formed every December between 1932 and 1977 on residual return behavior over the previous five years, giving 46 yearly replications. Multiplying replications removes part of the random noise.
The successive 46 yearly selections are not independent, so no statistical tests are performed on this experiment.

The results have some of the properties of a trading rule: they represent the average cumulative excess return, before transaction costs, that an investor aware of the overreaction phenomenon could expect following any December in which the strategy was tried.

Read as a demonstration of the effect's shape this is useful. Read as evidence the strategy was profitable it is not supported, because no significance test was run and trading costs were not deducted.

summary: The most quotable experiment in the paper and the least defensible as evidence. Both conditions on reading it come from the authors.
title: The five-year trading-rule experiment: no significance tests, no transaction costs

assertions.text: The price-earnings anomaly is Basu's observation that stocks in the lowest P/E decile earn larger risk-adjusted returns than high P/E stocks.

Three incompatible readings of it are in play. Most financial economists treat it as a statistical artifact of CAPM misspecification, with the P/E ratio proxying for some omitted risk factor that would eliminate the anomaly in the correct valuation model. The authors object that unless the omitted factors can be identified, that hypothesis is untestable.

Reinganum claimed the small firm effect subsumes the P/E effect, both reflecting the same unknown missing factors. Against this, Basu found a significant P/E effect after controlling for firm size, and Graham earlier found one within the thirty Dow Jones Industrials -- hardly a group of small firms.

The behavioral reading is Basu's price-ratio hypothesis: very low P/E companies are temporarily undervalued because investors become excessively pessimistic after a run of bad earnings reports or other bad news, and the price adjusts once earnings turn out better than the unreasonably gloomy forecasts; very high P/E equity is correspondingly overvalued before predictably falling.

This study's results support the price-ratio hypothesis -- but the authors note the argument implies the P/E effect is also mostly a January phenomenon, and that no evidence supports that claim except the persistent positive relationship between dividend yield, which correlates with the P/E ratio, and January excess returns.

On the small firm effect: work by Blume and Stambaugh, Keim and Reinganum largely redefines it as a losing-firm effect around the turn of the year, and this study lends further credence to that view, since losers persistently earn exceptionally large January returns while winners do not. Cutting against it: the companies in the extreme portfolios do not systematically differ with respect to market capitalization.

The results raise two unanswered questions for the tax-loss selling explanation of the January effect. If selling pressure disappears in early January and prices rebound to equilibrium, why does the loser portfolio rebound again in the second January of the test period, and the third and fourth? And why is the January effect so much larger in magnitude than the selling pressure that supposedly caused it in the final months of the previous year? The authors offer two possible answers: investors may wait years before realizing losses, and the market as a whole shows seasonality.

A live disagreement: Reinganum finds a considerably smaller January seasonal effect related to company size even after purging the data of tax-loss selling effects. The authors dispute this on the ground that his tax-loss measure uses only the six months of relative price movement before formation, so if many investors wait longer than six months to realize losses, the small-firm portfolio may still contain many losers.

summary: How the finding reshapes three neighbouring anomalies -- and where the corpus disagrees with itself and with others. There is no settled account here and this entry should not be read as supplying one.
title: What the reversal implies for the P/E, small firm and January anomalies

assertions.text: Shiller concludes that, at least over the last century, dividends simply do not vary enough to rationally justify observed aggregate price movements. Combined with Kleidon's finding that stock price movements are strongly correlated with the following year's earnings changes, this suggests a pattern of overreaction: despite the observed trendiness of dividends, investors seem to attach disproportionate importance to short-run economic developments.
Against it: Marsh and Merton hold that Shiller's findings result from his misspecification of the dividend process.

A further rival is that price variability reflects changes in real interest rates. The authors offer a counter-test: if so, the price movements of other assets such as land or housing should match those of stocks, and this is not actually observed.
The overreaction reading of Shiller is therefore contested in this corpus, and should not be presented as established support for the hypothesis.

summary: The other anomaly the overreaction hypothesis is offered to explain, kept separate because the evidence is contested and the corpus contains both sides.
title: Excess volatility as evidence for overreaction: disputed
